newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-PITMAN BIDS FOR THIRD AINTREE TRIUMPH.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-PITMAN BIDS FOR THIRD AINTREE TRIUMPH.

text.p: Trainer Jenny Pitman, the grandam of grand nationals, is at again with Aintree looming large on Saturday.
Victory in the Irish Grand National on Monday with Mudahim completed a clean-sweep for Pitman of nationals in England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
Now it's back to Aintree where she has already won twice, or even three times if you count Esha Ness, first past the post in the 1993 fiasco.
This time she relies on Nahthen Lad and Smith's Band, currently both around the 16-1 mark but likely to be shorter on the day as the British betting public piles on the cash.
Nahthen Lad has the better form and will be ridden by Jason Titley, successful for Pitman two years ago on 40-1 outsider Royal Athlete.
Smith's Band is described by his trainer as a "real National type," ideally suited by the 7.2 km test of stamina and 30 fences as challenging as are found anywhere, despite recent refinements.
Ex-champion Richard Dunwoody, who has also won twice previously, has the mount and given a clear round could lift the prize again if Smith's Band returns to his best.
But there are plenty of dangers in the likely 40-strong line-up, starting with 9-1 favourite Lord Gyllene who beat Mudahim earlier in the season, although critics reckon he may not stay the trip.

Go Ballistic (10-1) ran a splendid fourth in the Cheltenham Gold Cup last month and is very well weighted on Saturday. But he is still comparatively inexperienced and Aintree's big fences, Becher's Brook and The Chair to name but two, may find him out.
Suny Bay (12-1) won a recognised National trial at Haydock last month in excellent style, but he would not want fast ground and no grey horse has won the big race since 1961.
Irish raider Wylde Hide (12-1) has been the subject of some large bets and if the ground came up soft his chance would be greatly increased. Irish champion Charlie Swan has the ride.
Northern challenger Avro Anson (14-1) has been racing in better class, but he too is relatively inexperienced.
The usual pre-race parade of former Aintree heroes will be one short this year following the death last week at the age of 27 of Aldaniti, the winner in 1981.
Only time will tell whether Saturday's race will yield a story worthy of making into a film as was Aldaniti's triumph when ridden by Bob Champion shortly after the rider had fought off cancer.
But another Pitman victory could well bring the house down.
